acronyms.explanation: An open international information security standard that standardizes how to assess and report machine state (vulnerabilities, patch status, configuration compliance).
acronyms.exam_tip: Standardized XML schema used by vulnerability scanners (Nessus, OpenVAS) to automate compliance checking.

acronyms.explanation: An influential online community and non-profit organization that produces freely available articles, methodologies, documentation, and the definitive OWASP Top 10 web vulnerabilities.
acronyms.exam_tip: Must know OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities: Broken Access Control, Cryptographic Failures, Injection (SQLi/XSS), Insecure Design, Security Misconfiguration.

acronyms.explanation: A password-protected binary certificate archive format (.p12 / .pfx) capable of bundling both an X.509 public certificate chain and its matching private key.
acronyms.exam_tip: Used to export/import server certificates with private keys. Always password-protected to prevent private key theft.

acronyms.explanation: A decentralized computing architecture where each workstation has equivalent capabilities and responsibilities, sharing files directly without central servers.
acronyms.exam_tip: Security risks: BitTorrent clients frequently distribute trojanized software, consume bandwidth, and bypass perimeter firewalls.

acronyms.explanation: A JavaScript file that defines how web browsers and user agents can automatically choose the appropriate proxy server for fetching a given URL.
acronyms.exam_tip: Vulnerable to WPAD (Web Proxy Auto-Discovery) spoofing, where an attacker intercepts traffic by serving a rogue PAC file.

acronyms.explanation: A specialized cybersecurity suite that manages, monitors, audits, and secures superuser and administrator accounts (Domain Admins, root, cloud admins).
acronyms.exam_tip: Features: Credential vaulting, automated password rotation, session recording, and Just-In-Time (JIT) temporary privilege elevation.

acronyms.explanation: A legacy, insecure Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) authentication mechanism that transmits user credentials in unencrypted cleartext across the network.
acronyms.exam_tip: Insecure! Susceptible to packet sniffing. Replaced by CHAP, MS-CHAPv2, and EAP.

acronyms.explanation: An extension of NAT (also known as NAT Overload) that maps multiple private IP addresses to a single public IP address by assigning unique source port numbers.
acronyms.exam_tip: The standard form of NAT deployed in home and corporate routers: hundreds of internal hosts share a single public IPv4 address simultaneously.

acronyms.explanation: A cryptographic key stretching algorithm that applies a pseudorandom function (like HMAC-SHA256) along with a cryptographic salt across thousands of iterations to slow down brute force cracking.
acronyms.exam_tip: Key stretching technique: makes password cracking computationally expensive for attackers. Used in WPA2-PSK and disk encryption.

acronyms.explanation: A private telephone switching system within an enterprise that manages calls between local internal lines and connects them to public telephone networks.
acronyms.exam_tip: Modern PBXs use VoIP (SIP/RTP). Vulnerable to toll fraud, eavesdropping, and spoofing if not secured with TLS/SRTP.

acronyms.explanation: An application programming interface and standard file format (.pcap / .pcapng) used by tools like tcpdump and Wireshark to record raw network traffic packets.
acronyms.exam_tip: The primary artifact for digital network forensics, packet analysis, and reconstructing security incident payloads.

acronyms.expansion: DSS Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard
acronyms.definition: DSS Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard
acronyms.explanation: PCI stands for DSS Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard. It represents a core security concept, standard, or protocol in the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 certification blueprint.
acronyms.exam_tip: Recognize PCI (DSS Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) as an official objective standard under Domain 1.0.

acronyms.explanation: PDU stands for Power Distribution Unit. It represents a core security concept, standard, or protocol in the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 certification blueprint.
acronyms.exam_tip: Recognize PDU (Power Distribution Unit) as an official objective standard under Domain 1.0.

acronyms.explanation: A secure wireless authentication protocol that encapsulates EAP packets inside an encrypted and authenticated TLS tunnel using a server-side digital certificate.
acronyms.exam_tip: Only requires a digital certificate on the authentication server (RADIUS), not on client endpoints, making it far easier to deploy than EAP-TLS.

acronyms.explanation: PED stands for Personal Electronic Device. It represents a core security concept, standard, or protocol in the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 certification blueprint.
acronyms.exam_tip: Recognize PED (Personal Electronic Device) as an official objective standard under Domain 1.0.

acronyms.explanation: PEM stands for Privacy Enhanced Mail. It represents a core security concept, standard, or protocol in the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 certification blueprint.
acronyms.exam_tip: Recognize PEM (Privacy Enhanced Mail) as an official objective standard under Domain 5.0.

acronyms.explanation: PFS stands for Perfect Forward Secrecy. It represents a core security concept, standard, or protocol in the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 certification blueprint.
acronyms.exam_tip: Recognize PFS (Perfect Forward Secrecy) as an official objective standard under Domain 1.0.

acronyms.explanation: PGP stands for Pretty Good Privacy. It represents a core security concept, standard, or protocol in the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 certification blueprint.
acronyms.exam_tip: Recognize PGP (Pretty Good Privacy) as an official objective standard under Domain 5.0.

acronyms.explanation: PHI stands for Personal Health Information. It represents a core security concept, standard, or protocol in the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 certification blueprint.
acronyms.exam_tip: Recognize PHI (Personal Health Information) as an official objective standard under Domain 1.0.

acronyms.explanation: Any data that could potentially identify a specific individual (e.g., full name, Social Security Number, biometric record, home address, driver's license).
acronyms.exam_tip: High-priority compliance target under GDPR, CCPA, and HIPAA. Must be classified, encrypted, and governed by strict data retention policies.

acronyms.explanation: A standardized U.S. federal government smart card credential containing embedded cryptographic microchips used for physical facility access and computer system authentication.
acronyms.exam_tip: Hardware MFA token: 'Something you have'. Embedded with PKI certificates, biometric fingerprint data, and cryptographic keys.

acronyms.explanation: PKCS stands for Public Key Cryptography Standards. It represents a core security concept, standard, or protocol in the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 certification blueprint.
acronyms.exam_tip: Recognize PKCS (Public Key Cryptography Standards) as an official objective standard under Domain 1.0.

acronyms.explanation: The comprehensive framework of roles, policies, hardware, software, and procedures needed to create, manage, distribute, use, store, and revoke digital certificates and public keys.
acronyms.exam_tip: Enables asymmetric encryption, digital signatures, and secure TLS across the internet. Core components: CA, RA, CRL, OCSP, and CSR.

acronyms.explanation: A legacy email retrieval protocol (POP3 on TCP port 110; secure POP3S on TCP port 995) that downloads email messages from a server to a local client and deletes them from server.
acronyms.exam_tip: Port 110 is unencrypted. Port 995 is POP3S over TLS. Replaced by IMAP for multi-device synchronization.

acronyms.explanation: The traditional analog voice transmission phone system carried over copper twisted-pair wires.
acronyms.exam_tip: Vulnerable to physical wiretapping and war dialing attacks against connected dial-up modems.

acronyms.explanation: A direct Layer 2 communication protocol used to establish a direct connection between two networking nodes over serial cables, phone lines, or fiber links.
acronyms.exam_tip: Supports authentication via PAP, CHAP, or EAP. Used in dial-up and DSL (PPPoE) connections.

acronyms.explanation: An obsolete, insecure VPN protocol (TCP port 1723) that encapsulates PPP packets inside GRE tunnels with MS-CHAPv2 authentication.
acronyms.exam_tip: Obsolete and cryptographically broken! Known vulnerabilities allow easy decryption of traffic. Replaced by OpenVPN, IPsec, and WireGuard.

acronyms.explanation: A shared secret cryptographic passphrase previously shared between participating devices before communication begins (e.g., standard home Wi-Fi WPA2/WPA3-Personal).
acronyms.exam_tip: Used in home Wi-Fi (WPA2-Personal). Subject to offline dictionary attacks if password is weak. Enterprise Wi-Fi (802.1X/RADIUS) is preferred for businesses.

acronyms.explanation: PTZ stands for Pan-tilt-zoom. It represents a core security concept, standard, or protocol in the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 certification blueprint.
acronyms.exam_tip: Recognize PTZ (Pan-tilt-zoom) as an official objective standard under Domain 1.0.

acronyms.explanation: Software that may be undesirable despite the user giving consent to install it, often bundled with other free downloads (adware, browser toolbars, tracking monitors).
acronyms.exam_tip: While not strictly malicious malware, PUPs degrade performance, track web browsing habits, and increase attack surface.

acronyms.explanation: A PKI subordinate entity that verifies the identity of certificate applicants before requesting the Certificate Authority (CA) to digitally sign and issue the certificate.
acronyms.exam_tip: Does NOT sign certificates itself! The RA handles identity verification; the CA handles cryptographic signing.

acronyms.expansion: Research and Development in Advanced Communications Technologies in Europe
acronyms.definition: Research and Development in Advanced Communications Technologies in Europe
acronyms.explanation: RACE stands for Research and Development in Advanced Communications Technologies in Europe. It represents a core security concept, standard, or protocol in the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 certification blueprint.
acronyms.exam_tip: Recognize RACE (Research and Development in Advanced Communications Technologies in Europe) as an official objective standard under Domain 4.0.

acronyms.explanation: RAD stands for Rapid Application Development. It represents a core security concept, standard, or protocol in the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 certification blueprint.
acronyms.exam_tip: Recognize RAD (Rapid Application Development) as an official objective standard under Domain 1.0.

acronyms.explanation: A networking client-server protocol (UDP ports 1812/1813) providing centralized Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) management for users connecting to network services.
acronyms.exam_tip: Open industry standard: uses UDP ports 1812 (auth) & 1813 (accounting). Encrypts ONLY the password field in packet, while TACACS+ encrypts entire packet.

acronyms.explanation: A storage technology combining multiple physical hard disk drives into a single logical unit to provide data redundancy, fault tolerance, and improved performance.
acronyms.exam_tip: RAID 0 (striping - 0 redundancy), RAID 1 (mirroring), RAID 5 (striping with distributed parity - can lose 1 drive), RAID 6 (dual parity - can lose 2 drives), RAID 10 (1+0 mirrored striping).

acronyms.explanation: A dedicated server that routes and authenticates external remote clients connecting to an internal corporate network via VPN or dial-up links.
acronyms.exam_tip: Enforces MFA, network health checks, and least-privilege subnet access for remote workers.

acronyms.explanation: A type of malware that provides an attacker with complete covert administrative control and backdoor GUI access over a victim's computer system.
acronyms.exam_tip: Allows attackers to activate webcams, record keystrokes, exfiltrate files, execute shell commands, and pivot across the corporate network.

acronyms.explanation: An access control mechanism where user permissions are assigned based on their specific job role within the organization rather than individual identities.
acronyms.exam_tip: Best practice for enterprise scalability: users are assigned roles (e.g., 'Financial Analyst'), and permissions are attached to the role. Simplifies onboarding and offboarding.

acronyms.explanation: A legacy symmetric stream cipher once widely used in SSL/TLS and WEP wireless encryption.
acronyms.exam_tip: Cryptographically broken due to statistical biases in initial keystream output. Prohibited in modern TLS standards.

acronyms.explanation: A proprietary Microsoft protocol (TCP port 3389) that provides a user with a graphical interface to connect to another computer over a network.
acronyms.exam_tip: TCP port 3389. Prime target for brute-force ransomware attacks. NEVER expose directly to public internet; always place behind a VPN or RD Gateway with MFA.

acronyms.explanation: A wireless tracking technology that uses electromagnetic radio frequency fields to automatically identify and track tags attached to objects or badge cards.
acronyms.exam_tip: Used in building physical access badges and inventory tracking. Vulnerable to cloning and skimming; mitigated by using encrypted smart badges and shielded Faraday sleeves.

acronyms.expansion: RACE Integrity Primitives Evaluation Message Digest
acronyms.definition: RACE Integrity Primitives Evaluation Message Digest
acronyms.explanation: A family of cryptographic hash functions developed in Europe, most commonly producing a 160-bit hash value (RIPEMD-160).
acronyms.exam_tip: Used as an open alternative to SHA-1, famously incorporated into Bitcoin address generation algorithms.

acronyms.explanation: A financial performance metric used to evaluate the efficiency or profitability of an investment.
acronyms.exam_tip: In security: Used to justify cybersecurity spending (e.g., purchasing an EDR tool saves money by preventing costly ransomware payouts).

acronyms.explanation: The maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured in time that an organization can tolerate following a disaster or system failure.
acronyms.exam_tip: Dictates backup frequency! If RPO = 4 hours, backups must be taken at least every 4 hours so no more than 4 hours of data is ever lost.

acronyms.explanation: The foundational asymmetric public-key cryptosystem based on the mathematical difficulty of factoring large prime numbers, used for encryption and digital signatures.
acronyms.exam_tip: Standard key sizes: 2048, 3072, or 4096 bits. (Keys under 2048-bit are deprecated). Used in digital signatures, PKI certificates, and key exchange.

acronyms.explanation: RTBH stands for Remotely Triggered Black Hole. It represents a core security concept, standard, or protocol in the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 certification blueprint.
acronyms.exam_tip: Recognize RTBH (Remotely Triggered Black Hole) as an official objective standard under Domain 1.0.

acronyms.explanation: The targeted duration of time within which a business process and IT systems must be restored after a disaster to avoid unacceptable operational disruption.
acronyms.exam_tip: Downtime metric: 'How long can we survive being offline?' If RTO = 2 hours, systems must be fully back online within 2 hours.

acronyms.explanation: An operating system intended to serve real-time applications that process data as it comes in, typically without buffer delays (e.g., automotive brakes, aerospace, pacemakers).
acronyms.exam_tip: Requires deterministic latency. High risk: failure to process an event within milliseconds can cause catastrophic physical safety hazards.

acronyms.explanation: RTP stands for Real-time Transport Protocol. It represents a core security concept, standard, or protocol in the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 certification blueprint.
acronyms.exam_tip: Recognize RTP (Real-time Transport Protocol) as an official objective standard under Domain 1.0.

acronyms.explanation: S/MIME stands for Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions. It represents a core security concept, standard, or protocol in the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 certification blueprint.
acronyms.exam_tip: Recognize S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) as an official objective standard under Domain 1.0.

acronyms.explanation: The modern, highly secure cryptographic handshake algorithm introduced in WPA3 Wi-Fi to replace the vulnerable 4-way PSK handshake in WPA2.
acronyms.exam_tip: Immune to offline dictionary attacks! Even if a user chooses a weak password, attackers cannot capture the handshake and crack it offline. Provides Forward Secrecy.

acronyms.explanation: An open XML-based standard used for exchanging authentication and authorization data between an Identity Provider (IdP) and a Service Provider (SP) across web domains.
acronyms.exam_tip: The gold standard for enterprise web Single Sign-On (SSO). Uses XML tokens digitally signed by the IdP.

acronyms.expansion: Storage Area Network / Subject Alternative Name
acronyms.definition: Storage Area Network / Subject Alternative Name
acronyms.explanation: 1) High-speed dedicated storage network providing block-level access. 2) X.509 certificate extension allowing multiple domains/IPs on one cert.
acronyms.exam_tip: In PKI, SAN (Subject Alternative Name) allows a single SSL certificate to secure multiple domain names (e.g., example.com, mail.example.com, and 10.0.0.1).

acronyms.explanation: SASE stands for Secure Access Service Edge. It represents a core security concept, standard, or protocol in the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 certification blueprint.
acronyms.exam_tip: Recognize SASE (Secure Access Service Edge) as an official objective standard under Domain 1.0.

acronyms.explanation: A category of industrial control systems used to monitor and manage large-scale industrial, municipal, and infrastructure processes across broad geographic areas.
acronyms.exam_tip: Controls power grids, water plants, and oil pipelines. High-consequence targets for nation-state APTs (e.g., Stuxnet); must be isolated behind strict industrial firewalls.

acronyms.explanation: A multi-purpose NIST framework of specifications that standardizes the format and nomenclature by which software flaws and security configurations are measured.
acronyms.exam_tip: Combines CVE, CVSS, CCE, and OVAL to automate vulnerability scanning and compliance auditing.

acronyms.explanation: A PKI protocol designed to make the secure issuance and enrollment of digital certificates to network devices and mobile phones scalable without human intervention.
acronyms.exam_tip: Heavily utilized by MDM systems to automatically provision digital certificates to thousands of corporate smartphones and laptops.

acronyms.explanation: An architecture that uses software-defined networking concepts to dynamically route enterprise traffic across multiple WAN connections (MPLS, broadband, 5G).
acronyms.exam_tip: Centralizes management and deploys automated IPsec encryption across all transport links, lowering WAN costs and boosting bandwidth.

acronyms.explanation: A collection of software development tools, libraries, documentation, and code samples packaged together for creating applications on a specific platform.
acronyms.exam_tip: Presents third-party supply chain risks: developers must verify integrity, ensure SDKs are updated, and check for hidden spyware or telemetry libraries.

acronyms.explanation: SDLC stands for Software Development Lifecycle. It represents a core security concept, standard, or protocol in the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 certification blueprint.
acronyms.exam_tip: Recognize SDLC (Software Development Lifecycle) as an official objective standard under Domain 1.0.

acronyms.explanation: SDLM stands for Software Development Lifecycle Methodology. It represents a core security concept, standard, or protocol in the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 certification blueprint.
acronyms.exam_tip: Recognize SDLM (Software Development Lifecycle Methodology) as an official objective standard under Domain 4.0.

acronyms.explanation: SDN stands for Software-defined Networking. It represents a core security concept, standard, or protocol in the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 certification blueprint.
acronyms.exam_tip: Recognize SDN (Software-defined Networking) as an official objective standard under Domain 3.0.

acronyms.explanation: SE stands for Linux Security-enhanced Linux. It represents a core security concept, standard, or protocol in the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 certification blueprint.
acronyms.exam_tip: Recognize SE (Linux Security-enhanced Linux) as an official objective standard under Domain 1.0.

acronyms.explanation: A specialized hard disk drive or SSD with a built-in cryptographic hardware controller that automatically encrypts all data written to the drive in real time.
acronyms.exam_tip: Hardware-based Full Disk Encryption (FDE). Offers near-zero performance penalty. Supports cryptographic erase (sanitizing drive in seconds by wiping the media encryption key).

acronyms.explanation: A Microsoft Windows mechanism that handles hardware and software exceptions and errors in code.
acronyms.exam_tip: Attackers exploit SEH overwrites in buffer overflow attacks to divert application execution to malicious payload memory.

acronyms.explanation: A secure network protocol for transferring files, managing directories, and accessing files remotely over an encrypted SSH connection (TCP port 22).
acronyms.exam_tip: Runs on TCP port 22 (SSH). Provides strong encryption and authentication. Do NOT confuse with FTPS (which is FTP over TLS ports 989/990)!

acronyms.explanation: A family of cryptographic hash functions designed by the NSA and published by NIST.
acronyms.exam_tip: SHA-1 (160-bit) is broken and deprecated. SHA-2 (SHA-256, SHA-512) and SHA-3 are the current secure industry standards for data integrity and digital signatures.

acronyms.explanation: SHTTP stands for Secure Hypertext Transfer Protocol. It represents a core security concept, standard, or protocol in the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 certification blueprint.
acronyms.exam_tip: Recognize SHTTP (Secure Hypertext Transfer Protocol) as an official objective standard under Domain 1.0.

acronyms.explanation: A centralized security software platform that collects, aggregates, normalizes, and correlates log data and security alerts across an entire enterprise in real time.
acronyms.exam_tip: The central nerve center of the SOC. Key capabilities: Real-time correlation rules, alerting, automated compliance reporting, and historical forensic log analysis.

acronyms.explanation: An integrated circuit chip used in mobile phones that securely stores the international mobile subscriber identity (IMSI) number and related cryptographic keys.
acronyms.exam_tip: Targeted in SIM Swapping attacks: attackers socially engineer telecom carriers into transferring the victim's phone number to an attacker's SIM to bypass SMS 2FA.

acronyms.explanation: A formal contractual commitment between a service provider and a client documenting the agreed-upon standards for service uptime, response time, and performance penalties.
acronyms.exam_tip: Defines contractual uptime (e.g., 99.9% availability), maximum allowable outage duration, and support ticketing response time windows.

acronyms.explanation: The monetary financial loss expected every single time a specific risk event occurs against an organizational asset.
acronyms.exam_tip: Formula: SLE = Asset Value (AV) × Exposure Factor (EF). If a server is worth $100k and a flood ruins 50% of it, SLE = $50,000.

acronyms.explanation: A network file sharing protocol (TCP port 445) used primarily in Windows systems to provide shared access to files, printers, and serial ports.
acronyms.exam_tip: TCP port 445. Vulnerable to EternalBlue (WannaCry ransomware) on SMBv1. Never expose port 445 to the public internet; enforce SMBv3 with signing & encryption.

acronyms.explanation: A telecommunications messaging protocol component used to send text messages up to 160 characters between mobile phones.
acronyms.exam_tip: Insecure as an MFA channel! Vulnerable to SIM Swapping, SS7 telecom interception, and smishing attacks. NIST recommends app authenticators (TOTP) or FIDO2 instead.

acronyms.explanation: The universal internet protocol used by mail servers to send and relay outbound email messages across networks.
acronyms.exam_tip: Port 25 (unencrypted server relay), Port 587 (authenticated client submission via STARTTLS), Port 465 (SMTPS over TLS).

acronyms.explanation: SMTPS stands for Simple Mail Transfer Protocol Secure. It represents a core security concept, standard, or protocol in the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 certification blueprint.
acronyms.exam_tip: Recognize SMTPS (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol Secure) as an official objective standard under Domain 1.0.

acronyms.explanation: An application layer protocol (UDP ports 161/162) used for monitoring and configuring network devices (routers, switches, firewalls, printers).
acronyms.exam_tip: SNMPv1 & v2 transmitted community strings in cleartext! ALWAYS use SNMPv3 on modern networks: provides encryption (confidentiality), authentication, and message integrity.

acronyms.explanation: A messaging protocol specification for exchanging structured XML information in the implementation of web services across computer networks.
acronyms.exam_tip: More rigid and heavier than REST. Uses XML formatting and WS-Security specifications for encryption and authentication.

acronyms.explanation: A cybersecurity solution that enables organizations to collect security threat data and alerts from multiple sources and execute automated response playbooks without human intervention.
acronyms.exam_tip: Complements SIEM: While SIEM analyzes and alerts, SOAR automates responses (e.g., automatically isolating an infected machine, blocking a malicious IP on the firewall).

acronyms.explanation: A centralized organizational facility housing cybersecurity analysts who continuously monitor, detect, analyze, and respond to cybersecurity incidents using SIEM, EDR, and threat intelligence.
acronyms.exam_tip: Operates 24/7/365 with Tier 1 (triage), Tier 2 (investigation & remediation), and Tier 3 (threat hunting & forensics) analysts.

acronyms.explanation: SOW stands for Statement of Work. It represents a core security concept, standard, or protocol in the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 certification blueprint.
acronyms.exam_tip: Recognize SOW (Statement of Work) as an official objective standard under Domain 1.0.

acronyms.explanation: An email authentication protocol that enables domain owners to publish a DNS TXT record listing all authorized IP addresses allowed to send email on behalf of their domain.
acronyms.exam_tip: Prevents email sender address spoofing. Evaluated alongside DKIM and enforced via DMARC.

acronyms.explanation: Unsolicited, bulk commercial advertisements or malicious links transmitted across instant messaging applications (WhatsApp, Telegram, Slack).
acronyms.exam_tip: The instant messaging equivalent of email spam. Often used in social engineering and credential-stealing attacks.

acronyms.explanation: A standard computer domain-specific language used for managing, querying, and manipulating data held in relational database management systems (RDBMS).
acronyms.exam_tip: Vulnerable to SQL Injection if input is concatenated directly. Primary defense is Parameterized Queries (Prepared Statements).

acronyms.explanation: A profile of RTP that provides encryption, message authentication, and integrity protection for real-time audio and video communications (VoIP, video conferencing).
acronyms.exam_tip: Encrypts VoIP phone calls and video streams using AES encryption. Replaces cleartext RTP.

acronyms.explanation: A high-speed non-volatile electronic data storage device utilizing flash memory integrated circuits with no moving parts.
acronyms.exam_tip: Forensic consideration: Standard magnetic overwriting (zero-fill) does not securely erase SSDs due to wear leveling! Must use ATA Secure Erase or cryptographic erase.

acronyms.explanation: A cryptographic network protocol (TCP port 22) providing secure command-line access, remote administrative control, and file transfers over an insecure network.
acronyms.exam_tip: TCP port 22. Replaces insecure Telnet (port 23). Uses asymmetric cryptography for host/user authentication and symmetric encryption for session data.

acronyms.explanation: A legacy cryptographic protocol developed by Netscape in the 1990s to secure web traffic.
acronyms.exam_tip: Completely insecure and deprecated (SSL 2.0 and 3.0 are vulnerable to POODLE). Superseded by modern Transport Layer Security (TLS).

acronyms.explanation: An identity authentication scheme that allows a user to log in once with a single set of credentials and gain access to multiple independent software systems and applications.
acronyms.exam_tip: Implemented using SAML, OpenID Connect (OIDC), and Kerberos. Boosts user productivity, but compromising the primary SSO credential grants access to all connected apps!

acronyms.explanation: A standardized, structured XML/JSON language used to represent and communicate cyber threat intelligence (actors, TTPs, IoCs) in a consistent format.
acronyms.exam_tip: STIX is the language/format for threat intelligence; TAXII is the protocol used to transport and share STIX data.

acronyms.explanation: SWG stands for Secure Web Gateway. It represents a core security concept, standard, or protocol in the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 certification blueprint.
acronyms.exam_tip: Recognize SWG (Secure Web Gateway) as an official objective standard under Domain 1.0.

acronyms.expansion: Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus
acronyms.definition: Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus
acronyms.explanation: A Cisco proprietary AAA protocol (TCP port 49) used to manage administrative authentication and command authorization on network routers and switches.
acronyms.exam_tip: Uses TCP port 49. Encrypts the ENTIRE packet payload (unlike RADIUS which only encrypts the password field), and separates authentication and authorization.

acronyms.expansion: Trusted Automated eXchange of Intelligence Information
acronyms.definition: Trusted Automated eXchange of Intelligence Information
acronyms.explanation: An application layer protocol built over HTTPS designed specifically for exchanging cyber threat intelligence formatted in STIX.
acronyms.exam_tip: TAXII transports threat data; STIX formats the threat data. Enables automated machine-to-machine threat indicator sharing.

acronyms.explanation: TCP/IP stands for Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol. It represents a core security concept, standard, or protocol in the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 certification blueprint.
acronyms.exam_tip: Recognize TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol) as an official objective standard under Domain 1.0.

acronyms.explanation: A cryptographic ticket issued by the Kerberos Authentication Server (AS) to an authenticated client, used to request service tickets from the Ticket Granting Server (TGS).
acronyms.exam_tip: Targeted in Golden Ticket attacks: an attacker compromises the KRBTGT Active Directory account and crafts fake TGTs granting permanent Domain Admin access.

acronyms.explanation: A legacy wireless security protocol wrapper designed as an interim replacement to repair vulnerable WEP networks using WPA.
acronyms.exam_tip: Deprecated and insecure! Uses vulnerable RC4 cipher. Replaced by CCMP (AES) in WPA2 and SAE in WPA3.

acronyms.explanation: The cryptographic standard protocol designed to provide privacy, authentication, and data integrity over computer networks (secures HTTPS, LDAPS, FTPS).
acronyms.exam_tip: Modern secure standards are TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 (which removes legacy ciphers and mandates Forward Secrecy). Replaced broken SSL.

acronyms.explanation: TOC stands for Time-of-check. It represents a core security concept, standard, or protocol in the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 certification blueprint.
acronyms.exam_tip: Recognize TOC (Time-of-check) as an official objective standard under Domain 1.0.

acronyms.explanation: An open standard (RFC 6238) MFA algorithm that generates a 6-digit passcode based on a shared secret key and the current real-time timestamp (typically 30-second cycles).
acronyms.exam_tip: Used in smartphone authenticator apps (Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator). More secure than SMS codes; relies on time synchronization (NTP).

acronyms.explanation: TOU stands for Time-of-use. It represents a core security concept, standard, or protocol in the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 certification blueprint.
acronyms.exam_tip: Recognize TOU (Time-of-use) as an official objective standard under Domain 1.0.

acronyms.explanation: A dedicated, tamper-resistant cryptographic hardware microchip integrated into a computer motherboard to securely generate, store, and protect encryption keys.
acronyms.exam_tip: Enables Hardware Root of Trust, Measured Boot, and Full Disk Encryption (e.g., BitLocker seals encryption keys to the TPM to verify system boot integrity).

acronyms.explanation: A cryptographic mechanism used in DNS (RFC 2845) that uses shared secret keys and one-way hashing to authenticate DNS zone transfers between primary and secondary DNS servers.
acronyms.exam_tip: Secures authoritative DNS zone transfers (TCP port 53) from unauthorized replication and tampering.

acronyms.explanation: The patterns of activities, behavioral methods, and technical tools utilized by specific cyber adversaries or advanced threat groups to execute attacks.
acronyms.exam_tip: The pinnacle of the 'Pyramid of Pain': attacking or detecting an adversary's TTPs (e.g., using MITRE ATT&CK framework) causes the greatest disruption to the attacker.

acronyms.explanation: UAT stands for User Acceptance Testing. It represents a core security concept, standard, or protocol in the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 certification blueprint.
acronyms.exam_tip: Recognize UAT (User Acceptance Testing) as an official objective standard under Domain 1.0.

acronyms.explanation: UAV stands for Unmanned Aerial Vehicle. It represents a core security concept, standard, or protocol in the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 certification blueprint.
acronyms.exam_tip: Recognize UAV (Unmanned Aerial Vehicle) as an official objective standard under Domain 1.0.

acronyms.explanation: A cybersecurity process that tracks, collects, and assesses user data and activities using machine learning to detect anomalies indicating compromised accounts or insider threats.
acronyms.exam_tip: Detects unusual employee actions (e.g., logging in from an unfamiliar country at 3 AM and downloading gigabytes of sensitive customer records).

acronyms.explanation: A lightweight, connectionless Transport Layer protocol that transmits datagrams without establishing a handshake or verifying packet delivery order.
acronyms.exam_tip: Fast and lightweight: used for DNS (port 53), DHCP, NTP (port 123), and real-time streaming (VoIP). Vulnerable to IP spoofing and amplification attacks.

acronyms.explanation: The modern standard firmware architecture that replaced legacy BIOS, connecting a computer's hardware to its operating system.
acronyms.exam_tip: Supports Secure Boot: cryptographically validates bootloader digital signatures to block rootkits and bootkits from running before the OS loads.

acronyms.explanation: UEM stands for Unified Endpoint Management. It represents a core security concept, standard, or protocol in the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 certification blueprint.
acronyms.exam_tip: Recognize UEM (Unified Endpoint Management) as an official objective standard under Domain 1.0.

acronyms.explanation: A battery backup hardware appliance that provides instantaneous emergency electrical power to connected servers and network devices during power brownouts or blackouts.
acronyms.exam_tip: Bridge to secondary power: supplies power for 15-30 minutes, allowing graceful system shutdown or bridging the gap until emergency diesel generators spin up.

acronyms.explanation: A compact sequence of characters used to identify an abstract or physical resource on the internet.
acronyms.exam_tip: Superset of URLs and URNs. Exam scenarios highlight URI redirection vulnerabilities and path traversal attacks.

acronyms.explanation: A specific type of URI that specifies the network address and protocol mechanism used to retrieve a web resource (e.g., https://example.com/login).
acronyms.exam_tip: Protected using URL Filtering on Next-Gen Firewalls to block phishing links, malicious domains, and unauthorized categories.

acronyms.explanation: An industry standard connecting cables, connectors, and protocols for connection, communication, and power supply between computers and peripheral devices.
acronyms.exam_tip: Severe physical vector: Malicious Rubber Ducky keystroke injection, USB malware drops in parking lots, and unauthorized data exfiltration. Mitigated via USB endpoint port blocking.

acronyms.explanation: An all-in-one hardware security appliance that consolidates multiple security services (firewall, antivirus, IDS/IPS, VPN, content filtering, antispam) into a single device.
acronyms.exam_tip: Cost-effective, simplified security solution for small-to-medium branch offices. Contrast with enterprise defense-in-depth.

acronyms.explanation: The most common form of copper Ethernet cabling (Cat 5e, Cat 6) consisting of color-coded twisted wire pairs without internal electromagnetic shielding foil.
acronyms.exam_tip: Vulnerable to electromagnetic interference (EMI) and physical wiretapping. STP (Shielded Twisted Pair) or fiber optic cabling is preferred in high-EMI or high-security areas.

acronyms.explanation: An event-driven programming language developed by Microsoft implemented in Microsoft Office applications to automate repetitive tasks and macros.
acronyms.exam_tip: The primary vector for malicious Office document macro attacks. Enterprise GPOs should disable untrusted macros globally.

acronyms.explanation: A user workspace environment hosted on a centralized server or cloud infrastructure that users access remotely from a thin client or browser.
acronyms.exam_tip: Enhances enterprise security: all company data remains stored on central servers; if the user's local laptop is lost, no data resides on local storage.

acronyms.explanation: The underlying virtualization technology that hosts desktop operating systems on centralized virtual machines running in a data center or cloud.
acronyms.exam_tip: Centralizes patching, endpoint imaging, and security policy enforcement for remote workforces.

acronyms.explanation: A logical subnetwork (IEEE 802.1Q) that groups together devices sharing physical switch infrastructure into isolated broadcast domains.
acronyms.exam_tip: Core network segmentation control. Isolates guest Wi-Fi, HR, management, and IoT traffic. Prevents broadcast loops and restricts lateral attacker movement.

acronyms.explanation: VLSM stands for Variable Length Subnet Masking. It represents a core security concept, standard, or protocol in the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 certification blueprint.
acronyms.exam_tip: Recognize VLSM (Variable Length Subnet Masking) as an official objective standard under Domain 1.0.

acronyms.explanation: A software-based emulation of a physical computer running its own operating system and applications on top of a hypervisor.
acronyms.exam_tip: Secured against VM Escape (where an attacker breaks out of the guest VM to access the underlying host hypervisor) and VM Sprawl.

acronyms.explanation: VPC stands for Virtual Private Cloud. It represents a core security concept, standard, or protocol in the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 certification blueprint.
acronyms.exam_tip: Recognize VPC (Virtual Private Cloud) as an official objective standard under Domain 3.0.

acronyms.explanation: An encrypted communication tunnel extending across a public or untrusted network, enabling users to send and receive data securely as if directly connected to a private network.
acronyms.exam_tip: Implemented using IPsec (IKEv2) or SSL/TLS (OpenVPN, WireGuard). Full-tunnel routes all traffic through corporate network; split-tunnel routes only corporate traffic through VPN.

acronyms.explanation: A set of interactive telecommunication technologies which allow two or more locations to interact via two-way video and audio transmissions simultaneously.
acronyms.exam_tip: Target of 'Zoom-bombing' and unauthorized eavesdropping. Secured with mandatory passwords, waiting rooms, and end-to-end encryption.

acronyms.explanation: A specialized Layer 7 application firewall that monitors, inspects, and filters incoming HTTP/HTTPS traffic to and from a web application.
acronyms.exam_tip: Protects web servers from OWASP Top 10 attacks: SQL injection, Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), cross-site forgery, and path traversal. Placed in front of web servers.

acronyms.explanation: WAP stands for Wireless Access Point. It represents a core security concept, standard, or protocol in the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 certification blueprint.
acronyms.exam_tip: Recognize WAP (Wireless Access Point) as an official objective standard under Domain 1.0.

acronyms.explanation: A notoriously insecure legacy 802.11 Wi-Fi encryption standard introduced in 1997 utilizing RC4 encryption.
acronyms.exam_tip: Completely broken due to weak 24-bit IV reuse! Attackers can crack WEP keys in under 60 seconds with tools like Aircrack-ng. Never use!

acronyms.explanation: A dedicated system of wireless sensors that continuously monitors the radio frequency spectrum for unauthorized Wi-Fi access points, evil twins, and wireless attacks.
acronyms.exam_tip: Detects Rogue Access Points, Evil Twin APs, deauthentication floods, and unauthorized Wi-Fi bridging on enterprise premises.

acronyms.explanation: An active wireless security system that monitors the RF spectrum and automatically takes defensive actions (such as sending deauth frames to contain rogue APs).
acronyms.exam_tip: Unlike WIDS which only alerts, WIPS actively suppresses unauthorized rogue APs and rogue clients from communicating.

acronyms.explanation: WO stands for Work Order. It represents a core security concept, standard, or protocol in the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 certification blueprint.
acronyms.exam_tip: Recognize WO (Work Order) as an official objective standard under Domain 1.0.

acronyms.explanation: An interim wireless security standard created to replace broken WEP, introducing the Temporal Key Integrity Protocol (TKIP) and 128-bit dynamic per-packet keys.
acronyms.exam_tip: Superseded by WPA2 (which made AES/CCMP mandatory) and WPA3 (which uses SAE and 192-bit cryptographic suites).

acronyms.explanation: A simplified wireless network setup feature intended to allow home users to connect devices easily using an 8-digit PIN or push button.
acronyms.exam_tip: Critical security flaw: The 8-digit PIN is validated in two halves (4 digits and 3 digits + checksum), allowing brute-force cracking in hours using Reaver! Must be disabled.

acronyms.explanation: A legacy security protocol designed for mobile devices operating on the Wireless Application Protocol (WAP) architecture.
acronyms.exam_tip: Provides privacy, integrity, and authentication for mobile networks; superseded by standard TLS over mobile IP.

acronyms.explanation: A holistic, cross-layered cybersecurity platform that unifies security data across endpoints, cloud workloads, network traffic, email, and identity to provide unified threat detection and automated response.
acronyms.exam_tip: Evolution of EDR: integrates telemetry across endpoints, network, email, and cloud into a single unified investigation console.

acronyms.explanation: A flexible, human-readable text-based markup language used for storing and transporting structured data across diverse systems.
acronyms.exam_tip: Vulnerable to XXE (XML External Entity) attacks: attackers inject external entity references to read local server files or conduct SSRF. Mitigated by disabling DTDs.

acronyms.explanation: A fundamental binary logic operation (outputs true if and only if inputs differ) utilized universally in symmetric cryptography, stream ciphers, and one-time pads.
acronyms.exam_tip: Reversible: (Plaintext XOR Key) = Ciphertext; (Ciphertext XOR Key) = Plaintext. The mathematical foundation of modern ciphers and one-time pads.

acronyms.explanation: An alternative abbreviation for CSRF; an attack that tricks a victim's authenticated web browser into executing unauthorized commands on a trusted web application.
acronyms.exam_tip: Exploits user trust in an active session. Mitigated with Anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite cookie policies.

acronyms.explanation: A pervasive web vulnerability where an attacker injects malicious client-side JavaScript into a trusted website, which executes inside other users' browsers.
acronyms.exam_tip: 3 Types: Stored (persistent in database), Reflected (in URL/parameter), DOM-based. Used to steal session cookies and credentials. Defenses: Input validation, context-aware output encoding, and Content Security Policy (CSP).

ports.desc: Secure Shell, encrypted remote CLI & file transfer
Cleartext terminal emulation (Insecure, replace with SSH)
Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (Mail relay / outbound)
Domain Name System (TCP for zone transfers, UDP for queries)
Ticket-granting authentication service in Active Directory
Post Office Protocol v3 (Cleartext email retrieval)
Network Time Protocol (Critical for log timestamps & Kerberos)
Simple Network Management Protocol (v3 adds auth & crypto)
Server Message Block (Windows file sharing, target for EternalBlue)
Internet Key Exchange for IPsec VPN negotiation
Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service (Auth / Acct)
Remote Desktop Protocol (Microsoft GUI remote access)

crypto.details: Same key encrypts and decrypts. Fast. AES (128/192/256), 3DES, ChaCha20, Blowfish, Twofish.
Public key encrypts, private key decrypts. Used for key exchange and signatures. RSA, ECC, Diffie-Hellman (DH).
One-way digest for integrity. SHA-2 (SHA-256, SHA-512), SHA-3, MD5 (broken), SHA-1 (broken).
Slows down brute-force attacks on password hashes by looping thousands of iterations. PBKDF2, Bcrypt, Scrypt.
Uses ephemeral keys (ECDHE, DHE). If the server private key is leaked, past captured traffic CANNOT be decrypted.
Sender hashes message and encrypts the hash with sender's PRIVATE key. Receiver decrypts with sender's PUBLIC key. Proves Integrity, Authentication, Non-repudiation.

incident_response.focus: Policies, playbooks, team training, establishing jump-kits and communication channels.
Identifying security events via SIEM/EDR, triage, verifying indicators of compromise (IoCs), scoping impact.
Short-term isolation (disconnecting network cable, isolation VLAN) and long-term containment.
Eliminating root cause, removing malware, closing backdoors, changing compromised credentials.
Restoring systems from validated clean backups, reconnecting to production, heightened monitoring.
Post-incident review within 2 weeks: what went well, what failed, how to improve playbooks.

risk_formulas.name: Single Loss Expectancy
risk_formulas.desc: Asset Value multiplied by Exposure Factor (percentage lost in a single event).

risk_formulas.name: Annualized Loss Expectancy
risk_formulas.desc: Single Loss Expectancy multiplied by Annualized Rate of Occurrence (frequency per year).

risk_formulas.name: Mean Time Between Failures
risk_formulas.desc: Expected operational lifetime before an asset experiences failure.

risk_formulas.name: Mean Time To Repair
risk_formulas.desc: Average time required to repair and restore a failed component.

risk_formulas.name: Recovery Time Objective
risk_formulas.desc: Maximum acceptable duration of system outage before severe business harm occurs.

risk_formulas.name: Recovery Point Objective
risk_formulas.desc: Maximum acceptable age of data loss measured in time (e.g. 4 hours of lost transactions).

security_controls.desc: Hardware or software mechanisms (Firewalls, IDS/IPS, Encryption, Biometrics, Antivirus, ACLs).
Governance, policies, SOPs, risk assessments, security awareness training, background checks.
People-driven day-to-day security procedures (Security guards, backup rotation, log audits, visitor sign-in).
Tangible real-world protection (Fences, bollards, mantrap vestibules, door locks, badge readers, generators).
